title: Look at fallen nature without its guilt: pure nature differs as the naked from the stripped, negation from privation
source_text: XIX. Ut vero facile intelligatur, quid hujusmodi naturae status comprehendat, naturam lapsam intueri jubent, in qua quicquid praeter peccati reatum deprehendimus, hoc ad puram naturam pertinere profitentur. Quippe Regula solennis eorum est, naturam puram a natura lapsa discrepare sicut nudum a spoliato, qui non aliter differunt, nisi quod hic amiserit, quod alter nunquam habuit: ut proinde pura natura se habeat instar negationis, lapsa instar privationis.
pass_a_gloss: But that it may be easily understood what a state of nature of this kind comprehends, they bid us look at fallen nature, in which whatever we find besides the guilt of sin, this they profess to pertain to pure nature. For their solemn Rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked from the despoiled, who do not differ otherwise, except that this one has lost what the other never had: so that therefore pure nature stands as a negation, fallen as a privation.
pass_b_english: To make it easy to see what such a state of nature includes, they tell us to look at fallen nature: whatever we find in it apart from the guilt of sin, they say, belongs to pure nature.

Their set rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked man differs from the man stripped. The two differ only in that the one has lost what the other never had. So pure nature is like a negation, fallen nature like a privation.

choices.why: Scholastic pair: a negation is simple absence, a privation is the loss of something due.
